items.label: fc03-incident-note
items.front: What six things does the debugging laboratory require in the closing incident note?
items.back: Symptom, hypothesis rejected, minimal failing input, intended rule, verified repair, and missing evidence - written so another learner can reproduce the failure from the input alone, without your editor state.

items.label: fc01-evidence-lab
items.front: unionboot: how do you run the isolated merge-boundaries evidence lab, and what does it deliberately not do?
items.back: `node --test advanced-practice/merge-boundaries.test.cjs` from the repo root. It imports the real 3439 reference and proves boundary behavior - without grading learner starters, editing starters, writing reports, or downloading packages.

items.label: fc02-proto-fixture
items.front: Building a test record with an own '__proto__' key: why is an object literal the wrong tool?
items.back: A literal's __proto__ definition has special semantics (it targets the prototype), so it may not create the own data property you intended. Parse JSON instead - '{"__proto__":"data"}' creates an ordinary own key - and inspect Object.hasOwn on the fixture before drawing conclusions.

items.prompt: A learner's notes say only 'PASS 3439'. Why does the chapter call that worthless as evidence?

choices.text: PASS lines are cached from earlier runs, so the line may describe a stale result
3439 is the warm-up capstone, and passing it is expected of every learner anyway
The verifier never prints PASS at all; it only writes its results as JSON reports
Without the command you can't tell whose code ran; the default grades solutions

items.explanation: mode = starters ? 'starter' : 'solution' in verify.cjs - the default run grades the reference solutions/ unless --starters is passed. 'Write the exact command beside every result' is the chapter's rule.

items.prompt: A teammate changes the conflict branch to keep base 'to avoid losing data'. Why does D3 reject this repair even though it feels safer?

choices.text: It silently rewrites the published local-wins policy that the contract states
Base may itself be missing the key, so keeping base can throw at runtime
The change leaves conflicts unsorted, breaking that lexicographic guarantee
Keeping base is slower, because it forces a third property lookup for every key

choices: It silently rewrites the published local-wins policy that the contract states
Base may itself be missing the key, so keeping base can throw at runtime
The change leaves conflicts unsorted, breaking that lexicographic guarantee
Keeping base is slower, because it forces a third property lookup for every key

items.explanation: Product policy belongs in the contract, and the locally-deleted-key assertion exists to catch exactly this improvisation. The lab's lesson: code should not improvise a different policy during an exceptional-looking case. The contract says conflicts keep local, including local deletions.

items.prompt: The debugging lab's D1 hypothesis claims nullish coalescing discards empty strings. What do `'' ?? 'fallback'` and `'' || 'fallback'` each evaluate to?

choices.text: '' and '': both operators keep any string operand as it is, whether empty or not
'' and 'fallback': ?? only replaces null or undefined, || replaces any falsy value
'fallback' and '': nullish coalescing is the stricter of the two about empty values
'fallback' and 'fallback': both operators treat the empty string as a missing value

choices: '' and '': both operators keep any string operand as it is, whether empty or not
'' and 'fallback': ?? only replaces null or undefined, || replaces any falsy value
'fallback' and '': nullish coalescing is the stricter of the two about empty values
'fallback' and 'fallback': both operators treat the empty string as a missing value

items.explanation: The guide is explicit: nullish coalescing preserves the empty string; logical OR loses it. The hypothesis must be rejected by direct observation - that is the point of D1.

items.prompt: Why does the 3439 reference represent deletion with a fresh Symbol instead of a fallback string like 'absent'?

choices.text: Empty strings are nullish, so only a symbol sentinel survives the ?? operator
Symbols serialize to JSON more compactly than strings, keeping the result small
Strings compare by locale rules, so a string sentinel's equality is unreliable
A string sentinel can collide with a real stored string; a unique symbol cannot

choices: Empty strings are nullish, so only a symbol sentinel survives the ?? operator
Symbols serialize to JSON more compactly than strings, keeping the result small
Strings compare by locale rules, so a string sentinel's equality is unreliable
A string sentinel can collide with a real stored string; a unique symbol cannot

items.explanation: Every string is inside the value domain. The guide's fallback-collision case: base holds a value equal to the fallback string, and missing versus unchanged become indistinguishable. The guide also debunks 'empty strings are nullish' explicitly - they are not.

items.prompt: In capstone 3439, base, local and remote all hold different states for the same key. What does the merge produce for it?

choices.text: Remote's state wins because remote edits are assumed newer, and it is flagged
It is recorded in conflicts and local's state wins, even if local deleted it
It is dropped from both value and conflicts until a human resolves the merge
Base's value is restored, since neither edit can be trusted over the ancestor

choices: Remote's state wins because remote edits are assumed newer, and it is flagged
It is recorded in conflicts and local's state wins, even if local deleted it
It is dropped from both value and conflicts until a human resolves the merge
Base's value is restored, since neither edit can be trusted over the ancestor

items.explanation: The prompt's final rule: otherwise record a conflict and keep local (including local deletion). A conflicted local deletion removes the key from value while keeping its name in conflicts - the subtle case the worked trace drills.

items.prompt: The contract requires conflicts to be lexicographically sorted. How does the reference satisfy this without ever sorting the conflicts array?

choices.text: Object.fromEntries sorts its entries as a side effect of defining them
conflicts is a Set, which always iterates its members in sorted order
The verifier sorts the array before comparing, so its order never matters
The key union is sorted once and visited in order, so conflicts arrive sorted

choices: Object.fromEntries sorts its entries as a side effect of defining them
conflicts is a Set, which always iterates its members in sorted order
The verifier sorts the array before comparing, so its order never matters
The key union is sorted once and visited in order, so conflicts arrive sorted

items.explanation: `for (const key of [...allKeys].sort())` is the single O(k log k) step; conflict names are pushed in that order and everything downstream inherits it - a design worth stealing for 'sorted output' requirements.

items.prompt: Why does the reference assemble its result with Object.fromEntries instead of assigning result[key] = value in the loop?

choices.text: Direct assignment would replace the result's prototype with the string
It defines own data properties, so a '__proto__' key stays ordinary data
It deduplicates repeated keys, which the sorted key union cannot guarantee
It is faster, because it preallocates the result object's hidden class

choices: Direct assignment would replace the result's prototype with the string
It defines own data properties, so a '__proto__' key stays ordinary data
It deduplicates repeated keys, which the sorted key union cannot guarantee
It is faster, because it preallocates the result object's hidden class

items.explanation: Direct assignment would invoke the inherited __proto__ setter, and a string value would simply be ignored. The guide warns against explaining every special-key failure as prototype replacement: assigning a STRING to .__proto__ is ignored, not applied - the exact value type matters.

items.prompt: A record's side of the merge is read with plain `record[key]`. What misclassification does D2 demonstrate?

choices.text: Numeric keys are coerced to strings, so the keys 1 and '1' collide in the key union
undefined own values disappear, because bracket lookup skips undefined entries
An inherited property of that name reads as present, though the side lacks the key
Getters run twice, so their side effects double when the key is read for both sides

choices: Numeric keys are coerced to strings, so the keys 1 and '1' collide in the key union
undefined own values disappear, because bracket lookup skips undefined entries
An inherited property of that name reads as present, though the side lacks the key
Getters run twice, so their side effects double when the key is read for both sides

items.explanation: The reference's read() helper returns the missing sentinel unless Object.hasOwn(record, key) - lookup answers 'what value is visible', hasOwn answers 'does this record own the key'.

items.prompt: Worked trace: base {title:'draft', note:'absent', empty:'x'}, local {title:'edited', empty:''}, remote {title:'draft', note:'revised', empty:''}. What comes out?

choices.text: value = {empty:'x', title:'edited'}, conflicts = ['empty']: both disagree with base
value = {empty:'', title:'edited'}, conflicts = ['note']: a conflicted local deletion
value = {empty:'', note:'revised', title:'edited'}, conflicts = []: no key overlapped
value = {title:'edited'}, conflicts = ['note','empty']: deletions win both keys

choices: value = {empty:'x', title:'edited'}, conflicts = ['empty']: both disagree with base
value = {empty:'', title:'edited'}, conflicts = ['note']: a conflicted local deletion
value = {empty:'', note:'revised', title:'edited'}, conflicts = []: no key overlapped
value = {title:'edited'}, conflicts = ['note','empty']: deletions win both keys

items.explanation: empty: both editors agree on '' (keep it). title: remote still matches base, local's edit wins. note: local deleted, remote revised - both moved, conflict, local deletion wins.
